en: So now we had a closer look at naming
variables, properties, and functions and
methods. Let's now have a look at naming
classes.
Here we don't really have different cases to
consider. We should always describe the
object which is created when we instantiate
the class.
And that's important. Keep in mind that
classes typically are used to instantiate
something.
You can have static classes with static
methods, but typically you instantiate
something and therefore the class name
should reflect which kind of object gets
created.
Hence, classes might be named something like
User or Product if they reflect these
objects.
You can, as always, provide more details if
it makes sense and doesn't add redundancy.
So your User class could become a Customer
class, your Product class could become a
Course class, if your product is an online
course.
You can also use more than one word for
class names, but you should avoid redundant
suffixes like DatabaseManager.
It can be intriguing to sometimes use names
like this, but always consider that classes
are typically instantiated.
And if you do that, what is the instance of
a DatabaseManager?
If that's a person in your company, the
manager who manages all the databases, it
maybe makes sense. But if it's an abstract
thing in your code which just manages all
the databases your application uses, there
might be a better name available. Using
names like this might make sense if it's
mostly a static class full of utility
methods or anything like that, but typically
you wanna avoid them and you wanna go for
the clearer names instead, which can also be
instantiated.
And that's really all you gotta know about
classes. They should describe the object
which is built with help of the class.
